en: The Mahāyāna Sūtra of the Dharma Conch Explained by the Buddha in Response to the Questions of Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva,
translated by the Tripitaka Master from the Western Heaven, Chao San Dafu, Acting Director of the Court of Imperial Entertainments.
The Great Master of Elucidating Teaching, the Subject Faxian, translated by imperial decree: Thus have I heard:

At one time the Buddha was staying in the Universal Palace in the kingdom of Śrāvastī, seated upon a precious lion throne together with a great assembly of twelve thousand five hundred bhikṣus, as well as bodhisattva-mahāsattvas and hundreds of thousands of beings whose conditions for liberation had ripened.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mañjuśrī, empowered by the Buddha’s majestic spiritual authority, rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms in homage, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
He possesses great merit; how is it to be calculated?

Such great merit consists of immeasurable hundreds of thousands of koṭis and nayutas, fulfilling the aspirations of the multitudes to be saved when conditions ripen. How is it that the Tathāgata serves as the Dharma-conch for them?
At that time, having heard these words, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, saying: “Mañjuśrī!
Inconceivable conduct, great wisdom, and great kindness and compassion—these constitute great merit.”

Such great merit causes all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas to give rise to great skillful means, diligence, ethical discipline, vows, and practices, thereby accomplishing and attaining the supreme samādhi; they then contemplate all those whose conditions have ripened for deliverance as being none other than the Tathāgata’s Dharma conch.
The Buddha told the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī:
"If one were to take all sentient beings in Jambudvīpa and calculate the merit they would obtain by practicing the ten virtuous paths of action,
and if that merit were accumulated to a hundredfold, it would constitute the merit of a single Golden-Wheel-Turning King."

That universal monarch ruled over the four great continents and was endowed with the seven treasures, namely: the wheel treasure, the elephant treasure, the horse treasure, the mani-jewel treasure, the woman treasure, the steward treasure, and the military commander treasure; furthermore, he had a thousand sons who were courageous and majestic, possessed of handsome and noble features, and capable of defeating the armies of others.
"Mañjuśrī! That Golden-Wheel-Turning King possesses such great power.
Furthermore, Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva!"

Regarding all sentient beings within the realm of the four great continents, if each and every one of these beings were to possess merit equal to that of a single Golden Wheel-Turning King (Cakravartin),
and if the merit of all those beings were multiplied by a thousandfold, this would constitute the merit of a single Lord Śakra;
such is the power of the great majesty and merit of Śakra.
"Furthermore, Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva!

All sentient beings within the realm of the four great continents—each and every one of these sentient beings possesses merit equal to that of a single Śakra. When the merit possessed by all those sentient beings is calculated as a hundred-thousandfold multiple, that is the merit of a single Mahānārāyaṇa Deva;
such is the power of the merit and great majestic spiritual authority of a Nārāyaṇa Deva."
"Furthermore, Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva!

Suppose all sentient beings throughout the realm of the four great continents were each endowed with merit equal to that of a single Mahānārāyaṇa deity. If one were to calculate the total merit of all those beings and multiply it by countless hundreds of thousands, this would constitute the merit of a single Māra, the Lord of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven of the Desire Realm.
It is because such a Māra has planted roots of goodness in past lives and is born in that celestial realm of desire, possessing great sovereign power, that he is able to subdue the gods and humans."
"Furthermore, Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva!

Suppose all sentient beings within the realm of the four great continents were each equal in merit to a single Māra-king. If one were to calculate the total merit of all those beings and multiply it by countless hundreds of thousands, that would constitute the merit of a Brahmā in a dichiliocosm;
for that Brahmā practices the transformation of compassion throughout the dichiliocosm."
"Furthermore, Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva!

Regarding all sentient beings within two thousand worlds, if each and every one of these sentient beings were to possess merit equal to that of a Brahmā in two thousand worlds, and if one were to calculate all such merit multiplied by countless hundreds of thousands of times, this would constitute the merit of Mahādeva and Brahmā, the lords of a single trichiliocosm;
for those Mahādevas and Brahmā kings exercise compassionate transformation throughout the trichiliocosm."
The Buddha told the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī:
"You should behold this time when the kalpa is destroyed and is consumed by a great fire for the duration of one intermediate kalpa (*antarakalpa*).
At that time, Maheśvara and Brahmā, King of the Gods, send down a great rain, and its waters fill the trichiliocosm, reaching as far as the Brahma-heaven."

Furthermore, this great body of water was produced through the majestic power of Maheśvara and Brahmā; for such Maheśvaras and those Brahmās have planted great roots of goodness, attained birth in those heavens, and possess wisdom and great sovereign power.
"Furthermore, Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva!

Suppose all sentient beings in a trichiliocosm were each equal in merit to a Mahābrahmā or a Maheśvara of a single trichiliocosm. If one were to calculate the merit of all those sentient beings and multiply it by countless hundreds of thousands of koṭis, that would constitute the merit of a single Greatly Diligent Pratyekabuddha."
Mañjuśrī! Do not think that all sentient beings in the trichiliocosm possess the merit of a Great Brahmā King, or that they are equal to pratyekabuddhas, and thus consider them to be many.
"Suppose all the merit possessed by every sentient being in all the Buddha-fields of the ten directions were equal to that of a single pratyekabuddha of diligent application;
even so, it would not yet be much. Furthermore, Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva!"

Regarding all the merit possessed by all sentient beings in those Buddha-fields of the ten directions—where each and every such sentient being possesses merit equal to that of a pratyekabuddha—if one were to calculate the merit of all those sentient beings and multiply it by countless hundreds of thousands of koṭis and nayutas, this would constitute the merit of a single bodhisattva who has first resolved to attain enlightenment.

Mañjuśrī! Do not think that the merit of all sentient beings, multiplied by hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas, is equal to the merit of a single bodhisattva who has first resolved upon awakening, and thus consider it to be great.

Even if one were to take all the merit possessed by every sentient being throughout the entirety of the ten directions and the realm of empty space—whether born from eggs, from a womb, from moisture, or by transformation; whether with form or formless; with perception, without perception, or neither with nor without perception—even if multiplied by hundreds of thousands of koṭis and nayutas of times, it would not equal the merit of a single Bodhisattva who has first resolved to attain enlightenment, nor would it even approach it as something great.
"Furthermore, Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva!

If all sentient beings throughout the entirety of space were each to possess merit equal to that of a bodhisattva who has first resolved to attain enlightenment, and if this were multiplied by countless hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas, it would equal the merit contained within a single pore of the Tathāgata."
Within each and every pore of the bodies of all Buddhas, Tathāgatas, there are further ninety-nine thousand subtle and wondrous pores. Mañjuśrī!

If one were to compare all the merit contained within every single pore of such a Buddha-body against this [single mark], it would be multiplied by countless hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas; this is but a single secondary mark (anuvyañjana) of excellence among the physical parts of a Tathāgata.
In this way, each of the eighty minor marks of the Buddha’s body is fully endowed with the same merit as previously described.
Furthermore, Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva,

if one were to compare all the merit of the Tathāgata’s eighty minor marks by multiplying it by countless hundreds of thousands of koṭis and nayutas, that would equal the measure of merit in the auspicious lines on the palms and soles of the Tathāgata’s hands and feet.
In this way, each of these marks is accompanied by eighty secondary signs (anuvyañjana), which manifest beneath his hands and feet.
The verse says:
"Parasols, banners, and auspicious symbols; Garlands, hooks, crowns, and jeweled staffs."
The precious vase, elephant, horse, and tiger; the garuḍa and makara fish;
the tortoise, fish, and peacock; the kalaviṅka bird, the jīvañjīvaka and sārika birds; and the *cañcūrā* ruddy goose.
The parrot, the goose, the pigeon, and the barley; Mahauṣadha, Tenu, and the bull;
The ram, the dragon, and the king of oxen; The jewel mountain, the auspicious fruit, Pāṇḍava, and the deer king; The maṇi-jewel and the sharp sword.
The vajra, bow, and banner; the trident, plow, battle-axe, and hatchet;
the pestle, arrow, and noose; Yūna and Miga;
the lords Brahmā and Śakra; Dhṛtarāṣṭra and Varuṇa.
The Celestial King of Vast Vision and Great Learning, the Auspicious Day of the Great Sage,
the Deities of Fire, Moon, and Wind, the Lotus and the Sign of the Ten-Thousand Characters,
the Excellent Śaṣṭika Grain, and the Noble Seat of Nṛpa.
The mirror and the *kacchapa* brush, O Kauśika; the young gods and goddesses;
the drum, conch, and *mṛdaṅga*; the bracelets and the bells;
the earrings and the rings; the *muñjāra* and the *lata*.
The King of Wondrous Flowers, the King of Trees, the Lion of the Śākyas among the multitudes—
these and others, eighty in number, each named "Excellent," appeared beneath his hands and feet.
The Buddha told the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī:

"All such eighty minor marks (anuvyañjana), with all their merit, when multiplied by countless hundreds of thousands of koṭis and nayutas, constitute the merit of a single mark of a great man (mahāpuruṣa-lakṣaṇa) upon the body of the Tathāgata."
Thus, each of the thirty-two marks of a great man on the Buddha’s body possesses the aforementioned merit individually, and they appear clearly within the Buddha’s body.
The verse says:
"The mark of the *uṣṇīṣa*, with hair in a conch-like topknot, deep blue-black, glossy and curling to the right; the forehead broad and level."
The white tuft of hair between his brows emits light; his skin is wondrously soft and supple;
his eyes are wide like blue lotus petals; his teeth are dense and perfectly even, all forty being complete; and his four canine teeth are all sharp and pointed.
His complexion is white like jade or snow; his cheeks, face, and chest—his upper body—is like that of a lion.
His tongue is broad and long, and his physical form is wondrously perfect, like a nyagrodha tree.
The hairs on his body curl to the right; his navel is pure, deep, and well-concealed;
both his thighs are even and straight; his two calves are like those of the king of deer;
the soles of his two feet are level and full; and both his hands and feet are soft and supple.
The ten fingers are slender and long, all possessing the mark of webbed hands;
his gait is straight and forward; his tongue always perceives supreme flavors;
auspicious marks are attached to his body; and the seven places are all level and full.
The soles of his feet are level and even, always displaying the thousand-spoked wheel;
such a Great Man possesses these thirty-two marks.
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī:

"Regarding these thirty-two marks of a Great Man, if one were to calculate all the merit contained within these thirty-two marks against the merit of bringing sentient beings to maturity through conditions—the merit that fulfills the aspirations of those to be saved, which is incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*), inconceivable, immeasurable, unequaled, and unspeakably unspeakable-fold—it is for this reason that the Tathāgata says that the assembly of beings brought to maturity through the ripening of causes and conditions constitutes the Dharma-conch."
The Buddha told the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī:
"All the sounds of the sublime Dharma conch of all Tathāgatas are heard universally by all sentient beings throughout immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable worlds."
Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva!

It is not only the conch-like voice that is thus; the light from the Tathāgata’s body can also illuminate immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) worlds, enabling all sentient beings to behold the Buddha’s body—such is its inconceivability.
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva:

“Great wisdom and great compassion constitute great merit. All śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas possess skillful mastery in the practice of vows, great expedient means, pure observance of the precepts, and the attainment of the supreme samādhi.”
"Furthermore, Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva!
The Buddha-body is unconditioned because it is free from all marks; thus, it cannot be seen by any śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, or bodhisattvas."

The physical body manifested by the Tathāgata has two meanings: first, to fulfill the vow to save sentient beings made in response to past causes; second, because the conditions for the sentient beings to be saved have now matured. For these reasons, the Tathāgata manifests a physical body.
The manifested body is pure and subtle, causing all sentient beings who draw near and make offerings to obtain great benefit.
"Furthermore, Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva!
Because the Buddha’s body is supreme, his marks and signs are supreme;
because his marks and signs are supreme, his radiance is supreme;
because his radiance is supreme, his Brahma-voice is supreme.
Because the Brahma-voice is supreme, the teaching of the Dharma is supreme;
because the teaching of the Dharma is supreme, the Buddha’s conduct is supreme.
Therefore, the form-body manifested by the Tathāgata brings great benefit to those sentient beings.
"Furthermore, Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva!
Within the body of the Tathāgata, all marks are fully encompassed;

yet, according to the differences in the faculties, desires, and natures—whether sharp or dull—of sentient beings, the manifested form-bodies appear in various ways, enabling each being to draw near, joyfully hear the sublime Dharma, and attain liberation, such that they may constantly behold the Buddha even during their walking or standing."
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī:

“The Tathāgata, endowed with the qualities of an Arhat and a Samyaksaṃbuddha, has appeared in the world out of compassion for sentient beings, for the sake of benefiting, bringing peace, and conferring happiness upon immeasurable devas, humans, and all other living beings.”

At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mañjuśrī rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms toward the Buddha, prostrated before the World-Honored One, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I have now swiftly attained a great and wholesome benefit."
Thus it is, World-Honored One: you are unattached to the three realms, most honored and most supreme, benefiting all sentient beings.
When the Buddha contemplates all worldly phenomena, he is as immovable as Mount Sumeru and as unattached as space; he is inconceivable and beyond discourse, neither seen nor unseen.

When the Blessed One had spoken this sutra, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mañjuśrī, along with all the bhikṣus and bodhisattva mahāsattvas, as well as all the devas, humans, asuras, gandharvas, and others, having heard what the Buddha taught, were all greatly rejoiced; they believed, accepted, and practiced it accordingly.
The Mahāyāna Sūtra of the Dharma Conch Explained by the Buddha in Response to the Questions of Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva.
